prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned Romanian-language oeuvre, centred on large-scale prose and rooted in poetry, that builds an inner cosmos from memory, the body and dream

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Cărtărescu (B011) as the single credited writer, with Adonis (B021) and Can Xue (B012) as alternatives. The round-1 exchange did change the wording and the confidence of my case. The case rests on the common criteria as I can assess them from public knowledge. His voice is recognisable and not interchangeable with other writers. The dense, patterned prose carries a single metaphysical project built from memory, the body and dream. The Orbitor sequence (Blinding is its first part) and Solenoid, as publicly described, show formal architecture and imaginative and intellectual depth at large scale. The oeuvre is also complete enough to assess as a whole now. No rival on the shortlist combines scale, a coherent formal project and a cumulative structure that is visible even through translation as clearly. I have refined the citation along the lines several colleagues argued: prose carries the weight, and poetry is named as part of the oeuvre and its foundation without being the basis of the award. This matches the single-writer, single-language attribution and avoids a claim about the poetry that I cannot support. On the chair's question about a literary reason to prefer P000 or another candidate, I see none in the evidence before us. The remaining doubts are about evidence, not about the quality of the project. I cannot use the unanimity of the opening as an argument.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection stays as it was. Much of the achievement lies in Romanian rhythm, syntax and density, and I can approach it only through translation and general public knowledge. Whether the later volumes advance the project or only enlarge it is still unverified, and the exchange did not settle it. Olsson reads the late work as extension, while Mattson, Sem-Sandberg and Sward accept that only provisionally. I have no independent reading that could break the tie. If a Romanian-reading assessment showed that scale hides lapses of control, or that the density reads as mannerism in the original, the citation would have to narrow to the strongest long works, and Adonis or Can Xue could then be better supported. A second weakness is that the poetry and early work are thinly covered in my knowledge, so the foundation claim in the citation is itself provisional. The close agreement among members is not a safeguard against shared blind spots from translation-mediated knowledge.

responses.point: Olsson reads Solenoid and the late works as extending the earlier project. He says the citation should rest on prose alone if the poetry cannot be shown to carry real weight, and he asks Mattson to separate length from loss of control.
responses.response: His distinction is the right test, and I adopt it in the citation. Prose is the centre, and poetry is named as part of the oeuvre without bearing the award. I still hold his claim that the late work extends the project as plausible but unverified. The committee can reduce the risk by asking of each later volume whether it poses a new formal problem or enlarges an earlier one. I cannot answer that volume by volume from public knowledge. I will not let the claim of extension carry more than I can support. If it fails, his fallback of resting on the strongest long works is the correct narrowing, and I would accept it.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg would anchor the citation in the prose project, where the architecture is visible even in translation. He treats the poetry as foundation and not as basis, and he would reduce the translation uncertainty by obtaining Romanian readers' or Swedish translations' assessments. He also moved Can Xue up as a serious alternative.
responses.response: I agree on the anchoring, and my revised citation follows it. His proposal on evidence is more useful than another ranking. Judgments from Romanian readers, or a comparison of the best Swedish and other translations, would test the sentence-level claim that none of us can test now. I would add one condition: such readers should be asked about unevenness across volumes and not only about the quality of the best pages. On Can Xue, I agree that she is a serious alternative, and I keep her as my second alternative. His own condition, that someone show development within her mode, is unmet in my case. I can name representative works such as Frontier and Love in the New Millennium. I cannot show development across them from the evidence available to me, so I will not claim it.

responses.point: Palm ranks Adonis seventh. Her doubts are that Arabic prosody and the relation to classical forms are hard to judge in translation, and that his influence as critic and anthologist may be mistaken for the intrinsic quality of the poems. She would revise upward only if the case were made from the poems themselves.
responses.response: I accept the line she draws, and I tried to keep to it in round 1. She asks for a case from the poems. I can point only to the representative collections, Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses, and to the publicly described reshaping of Arabic poetic language through myth and fragmentation. I cannot demonstrate from the texts that the later poetry keeps its force, and I cannot judge prosody. So my answer to the chair's question is that the Adonis case does not yet hold without stronger Arabic-reading evidence. That is why he is an alternative and not my first choice. The reason is the weakness of my evidence, not a lower estimate of the poetry. I would not put him ahead of Cărtărescu without that expert evidence.

responses.point: Sward says the difference between Cărtărescu and Can Xue lies in the asymmetry of evidence, not in a difference of estimated quality. Cărtărescu's multi-volume structure offers visible stages of development, while Can Xue's partial translated corpus does not. She would compare the two if unevenness in Cărtărescu proved real.
responses.response: I think she has stated the situation accurately, and it is my position as well. I would add a caution to her own argument. Visible stages in a multi-volume structure show that development is possible, and they do not show that quality is sustained. That is why I treat extension as an open question. I agree with her fallback comparison. If unevenness were found, the question would be whether Can Xue's single method deepens over decades. I would want a concrete case for development before the comparison favoured her, and none of us has offered one. Until then the asymmetry she names justifies the order of my configuration, and I do not present it as a settled judgment.

responses.point: Mattson treats extension rather than repetition as the main basis for confidence in maturity, but she calls the risk that scale masks unevenness a question for close reading of the later volumes that the opening rankings do not resolve. She also keeps Carson as an alternative because of the central-versus-peripheral problem.
responses.response: I agree that the opening rankings are not evidence about the later volumes, and in this round I have not relied on them. On Carson, I think her central-versus-peripheral point is the answer to the chair's question about oeuvre definition. A citation would have to be limited to the original verse and hybrid works, and it would have to say so. Whether that leaves enough sustained quality is the question I would want argued before moving her above my alternatives, and it has not been. I also accept her view that readiness is not the issue: the major structures exist and can be judged now. The only open matter is how well we can judge them.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's sentence-level density, rhythm and syntax survives translation from Romanian cannot be settled from the public knowledge available to me. Romanian-reading expert assessments or the best translations could change the judgment.

Whether the later volumes of his multi-part works advance the project or only enlarge it is still unverified, and I cannot supply volume-level evidence. This is the central open question on sustained quality.
The weight of the poetry and early work is unresolved. The citation names it as part of the oeuvre and as foundation, which is a drafting choice and not a verified judgment of its quality.

Corpus coverage is partial and uneven in translation for Can Xue, Adonis and the other non-English candidates, so my comparisons rest on incomplete evidence. I cannot show development within Can Xue's mode, or argue the late poetry of Adonis from the poems.
Whether the close agreement on the first-place candidate reflects shared reliance on translation-mediated knowledge instead of independent confirmation cannot be determined.

No source in my profile states whether a co-opted member votes in committee, so the weight of this assessment in a six-vote model is a modelling assumption. I have not read the corpora independently or verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile, and nothing in the exchange changes this. Documented ties are collegial: election to the Academy in 2020 alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg, work with chair Anders Olsson, and the Permanent Secretary role, which carries no stated link to a candidate. My husband's public career and my own non-fiction on Wallenberg, Nobel and the Lenngren study have no stated connection to any candidate. My own literary practice is context, not evidence of a preference. These are my readings of the supplied profile and are not independently verified.
